results.title: Claiming Relevance for Social Science and the Humanities
results.content: This article addresses the issue of how Social Science and Humanities (SSH) researchers frame and argue relevance, where there are no explicit expectations to do so. This article seeks to explore how researchers in the social sciences and the humanities (SSH) express/make claims, in a broad sense, about the social relevance of their research. We pose the following questions: ‘how do SSH researchers from a selection of fields, typically associated with different positions on the nomothetic/idiographic spectrum, formulate relevance in research proposals?’ And – ‘How may these notions of relevance be related to the above-mentioned epistemological alignments in SSH?’ The result of this reasoning is that we have come to view relevance as a dispositional quality, or an affordance embedded in an epistemic context. Our analysis of the sampled project texts suggests that relevance expressions to some extent, relate to the nomothetic/idiographic division in SSH, as well as to the distinction between social sciences and the humanities, that the collective notion of ‘SSH’ tends to obscure.

results.title: A Case Study of Language and Literature Fields
results.content: Despite the great importance and function of the humanities, based on the evaluations, it is commonly accepted that humanities research is not effective in society and has a small share of science in different countries of the world.[5] Several reasons have been stated for the underdevelopment of humanities in society,[6–7] which are all valid and can be discussed, but we can also think about the problem from the perspective of how to evaluate research outputs – an issue that has been less attended despite its great importance.[8] Evaluation of the research and the researcher has many functions, such as creating an opportunity for the researcher to defend his/her performance and compensate for his/her weaknesses, gathering information needed for decision-making, policy-making and planning in research,[9] improving the performance and quality of research by determining strengths and weaknesses, optimizing the allocation of research financial resources,[10] providing guidance for designing and modifying evaluation criteria,[11] determining research priorities and designing relevant policies,[12] directing researches in line with the real demands of society, Evaluating different dimensions of research effectiveness, identifying effective research projects for commercialization, determining the quality of programs developed for research activities, and deciding on how to improve the quality of research activities.[13] These can be accomplished if we evaluate research outputs in proportion to each scientific field and use criteria and indicators that are compatible with the nature of these fields.
